cards.explanation: The answer is a spouse of their own. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says it plainly: "…each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." He gives his reason right in the verse: there is so much sexual immorality. Notice he says "his own" and "her own", friends.

The answer is False. Paul doesn't say only the husband. He says, "The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband." That little word "likewise" puts the duty on both of them, friends. It isn't just the husband's job.

The answer is True. Paul says, "The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife." It goes both directions, friends, and the "likewise" shows it. Neither one holds all the authority alone.

The answer is by mutual consent for a time of prayer. Paul says, "Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer." Count the conditions, bakers: both agree, it lasts only for a time, and it's for prayer. That's a pretty tight recipe.

The answer is Satan. Paul says to come together again, "…so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control." So the pause is for a time, friends, and then they return to each other. The text names Satan as the one doing the tempting.
The answer is False. Paul says, "I say this as a concession, not as a command." So he's not handing down an order here, friends. He's saying clearly what kind of statement it is.

The answer is gift. Paul says, "…each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that." He wishes all men were as he is, but he doesn't turn that wish into a rule. Different people, different gifts, bakers.

The answer is to remain unmarried as he is. Paul says, "It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am." He's speaking to the unmarried and widows here, friends. And he says "…as I am." so he's pointing to his own situation.

The answer is False. Paul says, "But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion." Staying unmarried was what he called good in the verse before, friends. This verse is for the ones who cannot control themselves.

The answer is that she must not separate from her husband. Paul says, "To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband." He marks it as the Lord's command, not his own, friends. That label matters.

The answer is stay unmarried or be reconciled to him. Paul says, "But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband." Two options, bakers, and he lays them out right there. Reconciled means coming back together with him.
The answer is True. Paul says, "And a husband must not divorce his wife." So the wife has her command, friends, and the husband has his. Neither one gets left out.

The answer is to stay and not divorce them. Paul says, "If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her." Then he says the same for a woman with an unbelieving husband. This is the part he labels "I, not the Lord…", friends.

The answer is True. Paul says, "Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy." He says it right after the part about the unbelieving spouse being sanctified through the believing one, friends. Holy, not unclean, is his word for the children.
The answer is False. Paul says, "But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." No chasing after them is required, friends.

The answer is bound. Paul says, "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." It comes right after he tells them to let the unbeliever go, friends. And he follows it with, "God has called you to live in peace."

The answer is how do you know whether you'll save your spouse. Paul asks, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" He asks the wife and the husband the very same question, bakers. I think it's a question that makes you stop and think.
The answer is False. Paul writes, "This is what I prescribe in all the churches." So it's not just for Corinth, friends. It's the same instruction everywhere.

The answer is to stay just as he was. Paul asks, "Was a man already circumcised when he was called?" and answers, "He should not become uncircumcised." So he stays as he was when God called him, friends. Paul says it again in verse 20: "Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called."
The answer is False. Paul says, "Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised." It's the same instruction for both men, friends. Each stays as he was when God called him.

The answer is commandments. Paul says, "Keeping God’s commandments is what counts." Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, bakers, and he points to commandments as the thing that matters. Clear as day.

The answer is don't let it concern you, but take freedom if you can. Paul asks, "Were you a slave when you were called?" and then tells them not to let it concern them, but if they can gain their freedom, to take the opportunity. So he gives both parts, friends. Don't be weighed down by it, and if freedom is possible, take it.

The answer is freedman. Paul says, "…he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman." A freedman is someone who has been set free, friends. So the one called as a slave belongs to the Lord as a freedman.
The answer is True. Paul says, "Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave." It's the flip side of the line about the slave, friends. Both belong to the Lord.
